items.titleEn: Arteta's delight at comeback and key contributions
items.summaryEn: Get Mikel Arteta's thoughts following our 2-1 win against Chelsea at Emirates Stadium
bodyEn: Mikel Arteta praised the contributions of Kai Havertz, Martin Odegaard and Bukayo Saka after the trio all continued to make massive contributions at the start of the 2026/27 season, this time helping us beat Chelsea.

After the shock of falling behind after 77 seconds, the German striker netted his third of the campaign to pull us level, a tally then matched by Martin just after half-time to put us in front and ultimately secure a big win.

The pair, plus Saka, who also has two goals to his name this term, missed large chunks of our title-winning campaign through injury, but now the trio are back and on song, helping us secure the Community Shield and three wins from three in the Premier League to continue our perfect start to the season, delighting their manager once again.

Reflecting on the 2-1 win against the Blues, Mikel said: “I’m really happy. I think it was an incredible game to watch, to coach. It was fascinating from start to finish. The level, the quality, the way we competed, the way we attacked, the dynamics and the fluidity. The threat that we generated against that really tough opponent. It was incredible.

“And then so many of the performances that we missed a lot because last year those players weren't available for us, so we took the game to a different dimension. The crowd was incredibly connected to the team as well, and when that happens, it's extremely difficult for the opponent to handle both things at the same time. So, a really happy afternoon.”
It hasn’t been too often recently that we’ve been forced to come from behind to turn a result around in our favour, but today it was necessary after Morgan Rogers’ early volley.

But Mikel was thrilled that his side stayed calm, kept plugging away and were rewarded with some technically brilliant goals, and some more that didn’t quite come off. Emiliano Martinez was forced to produce some top stops to keep his side in contention until the end, but the boss believes that there is plenty more to extract from his side, and ensure that there will be fewer nervy endings as the season evolves.

“We showed real composure, and we were really clear in the intent that we had, how we had to do it, and we showed incredible quality,” Mikel added. “We had to be patient, and we generated so many chances. They score, we score a goal and it’s disallowed. We continue and continue and continue, and that's why I think we got rewarded.

“We had so many [chances] as well. But for the very, very fine margins, we didn't manage to finish them. Those connections between players, that level of threat to occupy different spaces is very unpredictable, something that we are insisting a lot, and today it happened.

“You see where we are in relation to the level that is in the league, and how we can sustain that. We can still improve in many areas, a lot, and that has to be the narrative and the demands between ourselves, because we can reach better levels still, individually and collectively, and we're going to continue to do so.”

items.titleEn: Every word: Arteta's post-Chelsea press conference
items.summaryEn: Find out what Mikel Arteta had to say to the media following our Blues victory
bodyEn: Mikel Arteta was delighted with our display in our 2-1 win over Chelsea at Emirates Stadium on Sunday, maintaining our 100% start to the Premier League season.

The Gunners demonstrated great character to recover from falling behind to an early Morgan Rogers strike, with Kai Havertz and Martin Odegaard striking either side of half-time to wrap up the three points.
Mikel faced the media following the London derby in N5, and you can read every word from his post-match press conference below…

on today’s performance:I thought it was an exceptional performance. I enjoyed every minute from beginning to end. The beginning was tough, but I enjoyed it because the team reacted in a spectacular way. The conviction, determination, quality and intent we showed to help them constantly - it was beautiful. It was a fascinating game I think for the spectator as well, and I think we deserved to win the game which I’m really pleased with, obviously.

on the learnings after conceding first:There is something we do badly when we concede that goal, that we discussed before. But credit to them as well, that from that ball in the air, somebody is able to put the ball very close to the post and score against David, which isn’t easy. After that, we reacted; the crowd was incredible again, the atmosphere we generated within the stadium was so inspiring and so helpful, and it feels like a big win for us.

on what we are capable of this season:I think it’s an indication for us that we’re capable of performing even higher than we did last season. It depends on whether we maintain that desire, that humility, and continue every day to find a greater version of myself and the team. We still have a lot to grow and a lot to offer, and that’s the ambition of the team.

on Konsa’s big tackle on Rogers:A very English tackle, the crowd reacted immediately - you guys love that more than a goal sometimes! It was great, obviously. What Ezri has done - he’s played 11 minutes, he had five or six training sessions and the way he played man-to-man against an opponent like Joao Pedro - I thought he was phenomenal.

on how difficult the Premier League is to remain unbeaten:It’s going to be super hard, with the margins that you win games. You saw that a few days ago when we went to Villa Park, and it was a really tough one - and today again. Then we go to Sunderland, and it’s going to be so, so tough again. We know every week will be like this, but that’s what we’re prepared for.

on why Odegaard is playing at such a high level: First of all, he feels fit and confidence-wise, it’s the highest I’ve seen him. He has a point to prove from last season as well, from missing so much football. Kai is the same; Bukayo is the same. We missed so many attacking players last season for long, long periods - I’m not sure how many games they played together last season, but probably not many.

When you start to feel the chemistry they have between them and what they can produce, it’s great. But for me, he gets to that point because he’s enjoying his football. You have to enjoy what you do, to play with real intent, and that’s what I saw today. He was running forward; he took shots, created so many situations for his teammates - he was great.

on Kai Havertz’ performances this season:He looks happy. He looks settled, happy, and some great things have happened in his personal life as well. He feels fit, he’s training every day and has this routine right now. He’s scoring goals, but not only that - he’s also doing amazing work for the team.

on the strength of our squad:It’s no question that we have some great players. I believe in them and that they can improve, and they can have another version of themselves that is even better than what we’ve seen. If the team is better and the players are better, everyone will benefit from it, and that’s the objective.
on Mosquera’s fitness:He had a muscular issue, and we think it’s not too much. But we need to wait and see the next few days for how it evolves.

on Odegaard having a point to prove:A point to prove is in everything, first of all because he demands so much of himself. He wants to be the best, perfect, at everything. He’s so efficient in other things as well, and he’s playing with real joy. He was phenomenal as well.

items.titleEn: Konsa delighted with duel-filled home debut
items.summaryEn: Get the view from the home changing room after our Premier League game against Chelsea
bodyEn: After we came from behind to beat Chelsea, Ezri Konsa was delighted to have marked his first game at Emirates Stadium as a Gunner with a win.

The defender slotted seamlessly into our side alongside Gabriel in the heart of our defence, and found himself in the thick of the action straight away in an end-to-end encounter that swung both ways, but ultimately saw us clinch all the points.

The summer arrival more than played his part, contesting 12 duels, the most of any of our players, and won eight of those, his best figures in a Premier League game since December 2024. One of those brought his first big Emirates Stadium roar when he slid in dominantly to dispossess Morgan Rogers as Chelsea attempted to counter, a moment all the more special as it was on a friend and former Aston Villa teammate.
“I love duels. As a defender, I think these are things you have to cherish. For me personally, I love a challenge. I love being in duels. I had a few today and I'm glad I came out on top.
“[Rogers] is a good friend of mine, but on the pitch, it's a different story. I saw the opportunity to go in and make the tackle, and it came off.
“I really enjoyed the occasion. My first London derby and I thought the fans were fantastic, superb. They stayed behind us throughout the whole game; without them, these games are impossible.

“Conceding so early isn't great, and I know we take a lot of pride here in keeping clean sheets, but I thought the reaction was second to none, it was fantastic. It just goes to show the character and the mentality of this team.”

Ezri was the first change we’d had to make to our defence all season after Cristhian Mosquera picked up a knock against Villa on Monday, and despite only arriving a couple of weeks ago, he has quickly picked up our style and methods to make an instant impression on his new teammates and supporters.

“I felt right at home from day one,” he said. “The boys have been top, the staff have been top. Like I said before in previous interviews, this style really suits me - I love the boss' way of playing. The amount of quality that we have and the amount of quality I have around me makes things easier.
“I think it's important you go into different games with confidence. We've started really well but it's still early days. We're going to take it game by game and day by day.”

items.titleEn: Arsenal 2-1 Chelsea: Premier League – as it happened
items.summaryEn: Kai Havertz scored and made the winner for Martin Odegaard as Arsenal asserted their supremacyAnd now a third goal…There’s been a second goal at Hill Dickinson Stadium. Clickity click click click! Continue reading...
bodyEn: Match report: Arsenal 2-1 Chelsea

The first heavyweight encounter of the Premier League season was previewed in some quarters as the immovable object versus the irresistible force. Arsenal do not give an inch. Chelsea have been fun and free-scoring under Xabi Alonso. Yet that overlooked something pretty fundamental. The percussive force of Arsenal’s game when they have the ball and want to make something happen.

Chelsea landed a significant blow after 77 seconds when Morgan Rogers put them in front with nicely executed volley from the edge of the area. It was not only the first goal that Arsenal have conceded this season but one with rich narrative strands. Rogers was chased by Arsenal over the summer only to join Chelsea for £117m.

The story here was about Arsenal’s reaction. The sheer fury of it. For a blistering spell that culminated in Kai Havertz’s equaliser on 25 minutes, they threatened to blow Chelsea off the pitch. Arsenal’s confidence shone through. They had not lost to their cross-town rivals in eleven previous meetings in all competitions, winning eight, but it was rooted in more than that. They had too much for Chelsea and they knew it.
Arsenal FC have had a good day at two offices
Martin Odegaard
double quotation markBig game, tough opponent, really hard for us and we got there in the end.
Conceding early is never ideal but the reaction was top and I thought we played really well. It was a brilliant performance.
We showed our quality with and without the ball; I think the result reflects that.
[Kai Havertz] is a really smart player – he moves so well and takes so much of the defenders’ attention.
Ezri Konsa
double quotation markI felt at home from the moment I joined. Buzzing to make my debut at home and three points is the most important thing.
[On going behind] It’s part of football and what matters is how you react. We reacted fantastically. On another day I think we score three or four.
[On his tackle on Morgan Rogers] I thought: ‘If I’m going, I’m going all-in.’ It got the crowd going. If you get it wrong, it’s bad, but when you get it right it’s a good feeling.
Three games down, 35 to go. But the top two might be set in stone.

That’s a fine victory for Arsenal, who recovered from the shock of Morgan Rogers’ 2nd-minute goal to dominate a dangerous opponent. Kai Havertz equalised and then made the winner for Martin Odegaard with a gorgeous dummy.

Chelsea can take some positives, but they will lament a lack of precision and concentration in the final third. Yet they almost grabbed a point when Estevao’s late sizzler was beautifully saved by David Raya.
A roar of satisfaction echoes round the Emirates Stadium!
90+4 min It’s now or never for Chelsea Football Club FC.

90+1 min “I think your two Arsenal statement victories are the big ones but I’d put two against Real Madrid in as well,” writes Will Vignoles. “The leg in Madrid in the run to the final with that Henry goal and a defence led by Pascal Cygan, and then the Declan Rice game where Arsenal maybe ceased to be the punchline of European football and were taken seriously in the continent again.”

Was the first one a statement win or just joyously unexpected? Agree completely on the second though. In a way, even though they lost, the semi-final second leg in Paris that season was almost a statement performance too.
90 min Four minutes of added time.
90 min: Arsenal substitution Noni Madueke replaces the excellently Bukayo Saka.

Estevao charges inside from the right, lolloping Hincapie into irrelevance, and blasts a rising curler from the edge of the area. Raya leaps to his right and brushes it over the bar with his left hand. That is a seriously good save, the best of the match by a distance.

88 min James wallops a free-kick from 30 yards that flattens Declan Rice on the edge of the area. He gets straight to his feet, but I wouldn’t fancy his chance of doing any long division for next couple of minutes.
87 min: Chelsea substitution Danny Welbeck, once of this parish, replace Morgan Rogers.
87 min Arsenal love defending a one-goal lead and they have settled into a familiar 4-4-2 shape without the ball.
Joao Pedro turns smartly and is fouled 30 yards from goal by Zubimendi, who should probably be booked but isn’t.

83 min Rogers finds Palmer, tries to back up the play and is deliberately tripped off the ball by Rice. Palmer shoots wide from a tight angle, at which point Rogers kicks off with Rice. He’s got a point – it should have been a free-kick and a yellow card.
Instead, Rogers is the one who gets booked for pushing Rice.
82 min “Arsene Wenger’s 1,000th game, where Arsenal got absolutely larruped by Jose Mourinho’s Chelsea, was definitely a statement of some kind,” writes James Humphries. “‘God is dead’, maybe.”
81 min: Chelsea substitution Estevao comes on for Joao Pedro, who had a frustratingly woolly game.
[Edit: what the hell was I on about? Estevao came on for Pedro Neto.]

81 min “I like the cut of Chris Finnegan’s jib (69 min),” writes Matt Dony. “Let’s found the Campaign for the Limitation and Inhibition of Tzolis Over Real Impact Statistics. Not sure about the acronym, though.
80 min Arsenal’s next four games are away from home: Napoli, Sunderland, Ipswich (in the Carabao Cup) and Brighton.
Chelsea are home to Leeds (Carabao Cup) and Hull before visiting Brentford.
78 min: Arsenal substitutions Viktor Gyokeres and Mikel Merinoi replace Kai Havertz, who gave a masterclass in subtle centre-forward play, and the potential matchwinner Martin Odegaard.
76 min A Chelsea corner is headed away by Gabriel as far as James, 25 yards out. He pings a sweet shot that is headed away with masochistic glee by – you got it – Gabriel on the six-yard line.
74 min Now my ADHD brain wants to know – and share – Arsenal’s greatest statement performances. Old Trafford 1998 feels like the ultimate; Anfield 2001 would also be high on the list.

73 min It’s maybe a little excessive to call this a statement performance from Arsenal – but it has been a compelling assertion of their current supremacy, even more so because they went 1-0 down inside two minutes.

72 min Saka’s delicious corner takes a couple of ricochets at the near post and is grabbed on the line by Martinez. He was already on his back, not sure why, so he was fortunate the ball came straight to him.
70 min The resulting corner is flicked on by Havertz and then headed across goal and wide by a Chelsea defender.
Havertz has been majestic today, the player of the match for my GBP.

69 min: Good save! Havertz produces a deft flick through to legs of a defender to release Saka, who curls a thrilling first-time shot from the edge of the area. Martinez flies to his right to paw it round the post.
69 min Chris Finnegan emailed to suggest the assist for Odegaard’s goal should go to Havertz rather than Tzolis. I privately agreed, to which Chris responded thus:
double quotation markCall it extreme if you like, but I propose we hit it hard and we hit it fast with a major – and I mean major – leafleting campaign.
Can’t we just keep yelling at that bloody cloud?
67 min: Double substitution for Arsenal Piero Hincapie and Martin Zubimendi replace Riccardo Calafiori and Myles Lewis-Skelly.
63 min Palmer controls the ball deftly on the run and lifts a right-foot shot from 15 yards. It’s too close to Raya but Chelea are playing much better now.
Moments later, Raya dives bravely and decisively at the feet of Acheampong, who was moving onto Joao Pedro’s cute through pass.

62 min “Long way to go,” writes Colum Farrelly, “but there’s an impression that Arsenal know what they’re doing as a team while Chelsea are made up of skilful players recently introduced to each other.”
If it looks like a duck…
61 min Pedro Neto, who has been Chelsea’s best attacker from right wing-back, tees up Gusto on the edge of the area. He whips a first-time shot over the bar.
60 min: Double substitution for Chelsea Pep Chavarria and Malo Gusto replace Jorrel Hato and a visibly frustrated Romeo Lavia. Chelsea’s central midfielders are now Gusto and Reece James.
59 min Oh go on then.

double quotation markIt’s more than a little unfair that, when it comes to innovation, Sam Allardyce is mainly remembered for bringing the 568ml glass of white wine into the mainstream. He was the first to regularly play 4-3-3 in the Premier League; he was also one of the first to build cosmopolitan teams and to find marginal gains through nutrition, fitness, physiotherapy and data analysis.

Even on a micro level, he rarely missed a trick when it came to maximising results. So when Fifa and Ifab issued new guidelines for the interpretation of the offside law in late 2003, introducing alien concepts like ‘phase of play’, ‘active’ and ‘passive’, Allardyce’s brain became extremely active.
58 min Chelsea are having a decent spell of possession, perhaps their best of the match. A promising move ends when Acheampong’s cross is well claimed on the stretch by David Raya.
Arsenal break and Lacroix is booked for a foul on Tzolis. In fact, Tzolis has also been booked for waving an imaginary card.
56 min Palmer releases Rogers on the left. His heavy touch invites Konsa to make the kind of full-pelt lunging challenge that defenders love. He gets it spot on and the home crowd cheer lustily.

bodyEn: The first heavyweight encounter of the Premier League season was previewed in some quarters as the immovable object versus the irresistible force. Arsenal do not give an inch. Chelsea have been fun and free-scoring under Xabi Alonso. Yet that overlooked something pretty fundamental. The percussive force of Arsenal’s game when they have the ball and want to make something happen.

Chelsea landed a significant blow after 77 seconds when Morgan ­Rogers put them in front with a nicely executed volley from the edge of the area. It was not only the first goal that Arsenal have conceded this season but one with rich narrative strands. Rogers was chased by Arsenal over the summer only to join Chelsea for £117m.

The story here was about Arsenal’s reaction. The sheer fury of it. For a blistering spell that culminated in Kai Havertz’s equaliser on 25 minutes, they threatened to blow Chelsea off the pitch. Arsenal’s confidence shone through. They had not lost to their cross-town rivals in 11 previous ­meetings in all competitions, winning eight, but it was rooted in more than that. They had too much for Chelsea and they knew it.

Martin Ødegaard’s goal shortly after half-time proved the dif­ference – after a stunning feint by Havertz – and it continued Arsenal’s perfect start to their title defence. It is now three wins out of three. They will take some stopping. Then again, everybody already knows this.

It was possible to feel a blast from the past as Alonso lined up with three central defenders. Almost exactly 10 years ago, Antonio Conte brought Chelsea here and trailed 3-0 at half‑time. Cue the manager’s switch to three at the back, a click and a bolt towards the title. This was the acid test for Alonso and his team could not have made a better start. They had scored very early in Alonso’s first two league matches against Fulham and Brighton and it was the same again.

Arsenal offered £80m to Aston Villa for Rogers but no more. ­Chelsea went much higher and there was an inevitability about him ­showing up when it mattered. Arsenal did not clear their lines after a Reece James free-kick and when Jorrel Hato outjumped Ødegaard, the ball broke nicely for Rogers. The volley was threaded into the bottom corner. Could David Raya have done better? It felt that way in the moment.

Arsenal’s response was ferocious. It was the intensity and the physical levels. The Emirates sounded like a bear pit as the home crowd yelled after what felt like every coming together, every time an Arsenal player tumbled over. The equaliser was extensively trailed and it came when Havertz was allowed to drift along the edge of the Chelsea area from right to left. There was no challenge and his low left-foot shot beat ­Emiliano Martínez inside the near post.

It was a soft concession and out of keeping with the resilience that ­Chelsea had shown up to that point. Especially Martínez. The former ­Arsenal goalkeeper had thrown himself into a thicket of legs to keep out a low Ødegaard free-kick delivery, taking a boot to the head from Gabriel Magalhães for his ­troubles. He also saved brilliantly from the Arsenal ­centre-half shortly ­afterwards, ­keeping him out at close quarters after João Pedro had failed to clear a Declan Rice free-kick. On the rebound, Ezri Konsa hit the post before Riccardo Calafiori lashed the loose ball home. The goal check showed Konsa was offside and it was disallowed.

Arsenal created a staggering number of openings before the Havertz goal. Chelsea put their bodies on the line. Martínez got his angles right to deny Bukayo Saka; Wesley Fofana made a big block to thwart Havertz. After James had worked Raya from distance, Arsenal stormed to the other end and Hato leapt into a ­saving block on Ødegaard.

It was breathless stuff and it was as if Arsenal exhaled after the ­equaliser. This kind of tempo is surely unsustainable. Chelsea kicked out a foothold. Rogers curled past the far post and there was the crucial moment just before the interval when João Pedro got Pedro Neto away up the right. He cut inside and steered a low shot against the far post.

Arsenal cleared their heads for the second half and they were in front almost immediately. ­Ødegaard started and finished the move but it was all about the dummy from Havertz, who knew where his captain was when Christos Tzolis sent over a low ball from the left. Havertz’s move froze Fofana and Ødegaard had the freedom of the Chelsea area to ­finish. A couple of words about ­Tzolis: very polished.

Arsenal were not afraid to go long and fast from back to front through Raya; the challenges were numerous for Chelsea. They looked to their big guns to mount the fightback. Rogers almost got away only to be halted by a thunderous Konsa slide challenge. Cole Palmer flitted around the edges. He had a couple of half chances.

Saka forced Martínez into a fine save after a lovely touch from Havertz and Arsenal almost scored again from a corner, Martínez grabbing a loose ball when he was already on the ground. Chelsea pushed in the closing stages and they could point to the moment on 89 minutes when Estêvão, on as a substitute, exploded a drive from the edge of the area and watched Raya tip over. Arsenal did not deserve to drop points.

items.titleEn: Report: Arsenal 2-1 Chelsea
items.summaryEn: We came from behind to beat Chelsea, with Kai Havertz and Martin Odegaard again on target to maintain our 100% start to the Premier League season
bodyEn: Martin Odegaard continued his fine goalscoring form at the start of 2026/27 as he bagged the winner as we came from behind to beat Chelsea at Emirates Stadium.

In an early test of our title credentials, a second-minute Morgan Rogers goal saw us quickly on the back foot against an impressive Blues outfit, but we responded in the 25th minute when Kai Havertz came back to haunt his former club once again.

The tables were turned five minutes after the restart when Odegaard converted a big opportunity to put us in front, and after both Emiliano Martinez and David Raya exchanged big saves, we ultimately prevailed to maintain our 100% start to the season courtesy of a big derby day win.
BOLT FROM THE BLUES

You had to go back six years and six different Blues bosses for the last time Chelsea returned to west London with three points from our patch, losing the previous four by an 11-2 aggregate scoreline, but Xabi Alonso’s new-look side took just 77 seconds to show they were capable of turning history on its head.

A Reece James free-kick led to a bit of head tennis in the box, ending when Jarrel Hato nodded it out of the box into the path of Rogers. The most expensive English player of all-time was waiting to drill a volley low into the bottom corner past Raya, and he did just that as our shot-stopper conceded a non-penalty goal for the first time in his last 11 appearances.

Despite being stunned by the setback, it only prompted the Emirates faithful to urge them forward in pursuit of a swift response. They thought it had arrived on 12 minutes when a Declan Rice free-kick caused chaos inside the area, with Gabriel forcing a save, Ezri Konsa hitting the post and eventually Riccardo Calafiori poking the ball in, but VAR intervened after spotting an offside in the melee.
HAVERTZ SCORES AGAIN

The game was a rip-roaring, end-to-end affair with both sides happy to throw punches. Havertz and Bukayo Saka tested Martinez before Cole Palmer and James forced Raya into a pair of smart stops, but on 25 minutes we landed the all-important blow by getting back level.

Ben White and Rice sprang a move that found Havertz on the right flank, and he drove inside before letting fly with a low effort from 20 yards which Martinez got a hand to, but he couldn’t prevent it nestling into his bottom corner. It was the red-hot German’s third of the campaign, his sixth in his last eight club starts, and his fourth for us against his former employers.
But we couldn’t quite use that as a springboard to get the second before the break, and indeed it was the Blues who had the two best chances of the half’s remainder.

Rogers got into the area and whipped a dangerous shot wide, before in stoppage time Joao Pedro sprung a counter-attack and allowed Pedro Neto to scamper down the right flank, advance to the edge of the area and strike the base of the post as we departed for the break, thankful to still be level.
CAPTAIN CONVERTS
And five minutes after the restart, that proved vital as instead of falling behind a second time, we found a way to get in front ourselves.

Christos Tzolis was found on the left touchline and ghosted inside before playing a clever pass into the area. Havertz dummied, allowing it to run into the path of Odegaard, who had made a late burst into the box, and he coolly picked his spot past Martinez to register his third in four games this campaign.

But despite looking like they were only content to play on the counter throughout the first half, Alonso’s team enjoyed more possession in the second half, looked threatening, and Palmer should have done better when a big chance was only shovelled towards Raya.
KEEPERS COME IN CLUTCH

Saka came so close to making things more comfortable when a brilliant piece of play by Havertz allowed him to curl first-time towards goal but Martinez flung himself across his goal and his fingertips flicked the ball the wrong side of the post.

But anything our former custodian could do, our current one could do better. As the game ticked into the 89th minute, Estevao burst into life and sent a vicious shot spinning towards our net, but Raya instinctively shot up an arm and managed to palm it over the bar and keep us in front.

It was his first top-drawer save of the campaign to add to his collection from last term, and ensured that we made it three wins from three to kick off the campaign, and extended our unbeaten run against Chelsea to 10 games.
FACTS AND STATS
We have come from behind to beat Chelsea in a Premier League game for the first time since October 2011 (5-3), ending a run of 14 without victory when trailing to the Blues (D4 L10).
Chelsea have lost five consecutive away games against an opponent in the Premier League for the second time, previously losing six in a row at Anfield to Liverpool between 1992 and 1997.

We have won our opening three games of a top-flight campaign while also conceding fewer than two goals (1) for the third time after 1924/25, when we finished 20th, and 2003/04, when we went the whole season unbeaten.
Chelsea are the first team in Premier League history to score inside the opening five minutes in each of their first three games of the season.
Chelsea’s opening goal after 77 seconds was the earliest conceded by Arsenal in the Premier League since August 2023, when Andreas Pereira netted for Fulham after 57 seconds.

Among those to have previously played for Chelsea in the competition, only two have scored more Premier League goals against the Blues after leaving the club than Kai Havertz (3): Mohamed Salah (5) and Kevin De Bruyne (5).
Martin Odegaard has scored three goals in four appearances across all competitions this season – this after netting just once in 36 outings last term.

There were nine shots on target registered in this game inside the first 25 minutes, culminating with Kai Havertz’s goal – only one Premier League game on record (since 2003/04) has seen more shots on target in the opening 25 minutes (11 in West Ham vs Sunderland in May 2011).
WHAT'S NEXT

We'll now prepare to get our Champions League campaign underway with a solid start at Napoli on Wednesday, before we're back in league action next weekend when we make the trip to Sunderland on Saturday. Then we switch gears to the Carabao Cup, when we are again on the road as we head to Ipswich Town on Tuesday, September 15.

bodyEn: Our young Gunners secured their first U18 Premier League South win of the season, beating Southampton 1-0 at the Sobha Realty Training Centre.
Maalik Hashi’s first-half goal proved the difference, with his effort finding the far corner via the woodwork.
Our under-18s held on to earn victory against a Saints side that had started the day unbeaten, with three points moving us up to 10th place.

items.titleEn: Baum reacts to incredible winning goal
items.summaryEn: Our winger enjoyed a debut to remember in our WSL win over Brighton
bodyEn: As debut goals go, they don't come much better than Lisa Baum's winner against Brighton on the opening weekend of the Women's Super League.
The German teenager, starting on the left, rifled her effort in off the crossbar in front of our travelling support to give us all three points at Broadfield Stadium.
So what does it feel like to score on your first Arsenal appearance? Lisa has the insight.
"I'm just happy that we have three points and won the game. And of course, to score on the debut, I'm just even happier.
"I just received the ball in the middle and then I just carried on and dribbled and then I just looked for the opportunity to shoot in the top corner, so I just took it in and scored."
And celebrating in front of our travelling support? She said: "It's really insane. It was so loud and my teammates were with me, so it's just even better."

Having grown up playing football in Germany, Lisa made the move from Leipzig to north London this summer. Having played her first 63 minutes of WSL football, the winger compared playing in her homeland and England.

She said: "I think it's quite a different level. Just intensity, time, you don't have a lot of time anymore. But I think you adapt quite well and the more games we play, the better it's going to be. So I'm just happy to be here and help us for the next wins or next games.
"Brighton did a good job of defending us, and to attack us as well. But I'm just happy, I think I settled in quite well. Everybody was so nice to me."
Lisa can look forward to her home debut in front of a big crowd as we play at Emirates Stadium next weekend against Crystal Palace.
"I'm very excited to play at Emirates in front of even more fans. Can't wait, I'm looking forward to it!"

items.titleEn: Renée delighted for debutants in win at Brighton
items.summaryEn: Slegers reacts to our 1-0 victory over Brighton to kick off the WSL season
bodyEn: Renée Slegers said she was thrilled for our newest stars as Lisa Baum scored an incredible winning goal on her debut against Brighton.
Making her first appearance in the Women's Super League after moving from Leipzig this summer, the 19-year-old winger lashed into the net to give us the 1-0 victory at Broadfield Stadium.
Lisa was one of four new faces in the starting line-up, alongside Georgia Stanway, Ona Batlle and Misa Rodriguez, who was forced into an early save to keep the score level.
After the match, Renée expressed her delight for the debutants and the whole squad as we picked up our first win at Brighton in three seasons.
"I'm so happy for all of them," Renée said. "I'm also happy for everyone else that the season has started, because this is what we've been working towards.
"Misa was amazing, her presence in goal was really good. She communicates from behind, she's always active, and she saves us, so she had a big impact.
"Then Lisa, she's a very young player, but she doesn't come across as that young. She's very mature in the way she thinks, the way she plays.

"She was really calm today, she's making her debut. It's not easy, she's young, we're starting her, but she scores that goal, a fantastic goal. I think she shows her skill and what she can do for us, and in front of the fans. So it was a special moment for her."
Lisa is one of eight new faces in N5 for the 26/27 campaign, and our manager thinks the whole squad has come together quickly, which can only be a positive as we battle across three competitions.

"We've been working really hard in pre-season, of course, on our football game model, how we want to bring that all together with different player strengths. But also off the pitch, connecting as a group, getting to know each other, understanding what we're a part of. The group has been amazing, so they've been investing a lot in themselves, in each other.
"It feels like this group has been together for much longer than five weeks. So that's a really good sign."
We had chances to add to the scoresheet but, in the end, saw out the match to pick up three points and a clean sheet.

Assessing the victory in Sussex, Slegers said: "The win is most important, so we get the three points. We know how hard it is, the WSL opener. I think I saw it in the other games as well, it can be quite chaotic, hectic.

"I think we controlled the game well, specifically spells in the first half. I think we spent quite some time without the ball, which we want to minimise. It was an okay performance; I think there were highs and lows.

We definitely can do more, want to do more and need to do more. But like I said, this being the opener, Brighton away, which is a difficult game. Getting the win over the line is something we've been talking about, keeping a clean sheet, so I'm happy with that."

items.titleEn: Match Report: Brighton 0-1 Arsenal Women
items.summaryEn: All the details from our Women's Super League opener against Brighton
bodyEn: Lisa Baum's sensational debut strike gave us all three points as we defeated Brighton & Hove Albion 1-0 on the opening day of the Women's Super League season.
The 19-year-old unleashed a rocket after just 10 minutes, which proved to be enough to win at the Broadfield Stadium, where we'd failed to claim victory on our past two WSL visits.
BAUM MAKES HER MARK
We had four debutants in the starting line-up for our WSL opener and one of those, Misa Rodriguez, was put to the test within five minutes of kick-off.

A fine ball over the top from Brighton goalkeeper Chiamaka Nnadozie found Kiko Seike, who was able to get beyond Ona Batlle and get her shot away, only to find Misa in the way. Our goalkeeper plunged low to her right to make the stop and prevent us from falling behind.

But it was another newbie who made the breakthrough with a sensational solo strike. After winning the ball back just inside the Brighton half, Baum picked up possession before weaving her way into the box and unleashing a powerful effort, which cannoned off the underside of the crossbar and into the net.

Three minutes later, we should've had a second. Good pressing from Olivia Smith forced Manuela Vanegas to give up possession, allowing the Canadian to square the ball for Alessia Russo. Our England star had time inside the box but could only fire over the bar in front of our travelling support.
CHANCES AT BOTH ENDS
Both sides continued to attack in the Sussex sunshine. Seike was a consistent threat for Brighton, but our new full-back Batlle was more than a match for the Japanese winger.
Down the other end, Russo had a second opportunity to open her account for 26/27, racing through one-on-one before her shot was stopped by Nnadozie, who was out quickly to deny our number 23.
Our midfield was showing its strength at Broadfield Stadium, with Mariona Caldentey next to go after creating space on the edge of the box. Her effort was comfortably saved by the busy Nnadozie.

The Seagulls, under new management of Arturo Ruiz, then had their best opening just before the break. A long ball into the box was knocked down by Vanegas to Fran Kirby, whose first-time effort went high over the bar.
SECOND HALF BATTLE

The Seagulls were still searching for an equaliser and began the second half with intent. Marisa Olislagers pinged her effort into a dangerous area inside the box, only to find the strong hands of Misa in the way.

After a bright Brighton start, we went back to dominating the ball and creating chances. Baum worked her magic to create an opening inside the box, firing a low cross that Vanegas eventually cleared off the line. Moments later, Kim Little had a go, firing her effort on target and into the gloves of Nnadozie.

Baum, who we signed from Leipzig in the summer, was settling into life in the WSL very quickly. The German showed off her dribbling skills to drift into the box before getting her latest shot away. This one lacked the precision of her earlier goal and was fired straight at Nnadozie.

Seike was providing the biggest threat for the hosts. Her pace on the break was causing problems and she almost equalised. The Japanese got a shot away just inside the box, which took a deflection off Batlle and went just wide.
SEEING IT OUT
A positive debut Baum came to an end and was replaced by Catilin Foord, with the Australian getting into the action immediately, firing an effort over the bar.
Down the other end, full-back Charlie Rule went close for the Seagulls - her first time effort going just over the bar.
The game became stretched and we almost added a second on the break. Russo was able to find substitute Stina Blackstenius, who fired her effort low, but found Nnadozie in inspired form.
With six minutes added on by referee Kirsty Dowle, we saw out the contest by controlling most of possession and getting off to an ideal start to the campaign.

items.titleEn: Preview: Arsenal v Chelsea
items.summaryEn: Get all the lowdown on our Sunday opponents as we take on Chelsea
bodyEn: After picking up our second Premier League win of the season at Aston Villa, we return to Emirates Stadium to take on Chelsea in a huge London derby.
Both sides have made a perfect start to the league season, with our opponents beating Fulham and Brighton in their first two matches.
Chelsea were one of the busiest clubs in the transfer window, but after that closed this week, it's all about the football as the two sides go head-to-head on Sunday at 4.30pm.
ALONSO SETTLES QUICKLY
Chelsea missed out on European football last season as new manager Xabi Alonso became the sixth permanent boss in six years.

The Spaniard, who grew up in the same region as our boss, Mikel Arteta, brought in 11 players, including former Gunners Emiliano Martinez and Danny Welbeck, as well as Premier League players Morgan Rogers, Jordan Henderson and Maxence Lacroix.
It's been so far, so good, for the former Real Madrid and Bayer Leverkusen boss, who picked up two victories in his opening two games as manager.

It started with west London derby success against Fulham, with front three Morgan Rogers, Cole Palmer and Joao Pedro all finding the net. They followed that up with a thrilling 4-3 triumph over Brighton.
It means that Chelsea join us with six points out of six going into their trip north, where they last beat us 2-0 in August 2021.
WHAT THE MANAGERS SAY

Arteta: "I love my players, that's what I can say. I think at the end of the season we'll put everybody in their place and let's trust them. Let's make sure that we are right behind them and we do everything we can to help the incredible talent that they have.

"The two games that they [Chelsea] played, they scored very, very early and that changes the momentum and the shift of the game. But they are capable and he [Alonso] is capable of playing in various ways. That's been a really successful match so far."
Alonso: "We can be very happy with the whole transfer window. What we started talking about in May/early June - many things we have.
"It is a very balanced phase one we have made in this transfer window. Phase one is completed; it's a good one for now and for the future."
TEAM NEWS

During his pre-match press conference, Mikel Arteta said that Bruno Guimaraes picked up a knock in our 1-0 win at Aston Villa, with a decision on his inclusion to come this weekend. He also said the same of Cristhian Mosquera, who was forced off at Villa Park. Elsewhere, Jurrien Timber was in training as he continues his recovery. William Saliba is a longer-term absentee, with Mikel positive about his development.
He said: "The progression has been really positive in the last few weeks, but we need to wait and see how that one reacts when we start to put some load into it."

As for Chelsea, they are waiting on a late fitness test of midfielder Moises Caicedo, who went off in their 4-3 victory over Brighton & Hove Albion. The Blues will also be without Jordan Henderson, who picked up an injury during the World Cup with England, but Alonso admitted he's getting closer and closer to first-team action.
TALKING TACTICS

Adrian Clarke: Chelsea’s new-look front three are dripping with match-winning talent. England duo Morgan Rogers and Cole Palmer love to float around between the lines in support of striker Joao Pedro, and as a trio they are flying right now. Across just 180 minutes of Premier League football alongside one another, they have delivered five goals and four assists combined.

Chelsea’s attacking wingbacks have also been bright, with Pedro Neto and Jorrel Hato catching the eye. Portugal international Neto was super-dangerous inside the final third last time out but is not a natural defender. So, will Alonso trust him in that role? If Neto starts, it will certainly signify the Spaniard’s intent to attack us at every opportunity.

Central midfield looks like an area of possible weakness. Enzo Fernandez has left the club, while Moises Caicedo has also suffered with injury issues early in the campaign. This means the likes of Romeo Lavia, Malo Gusto, Reece James and Valentin Barco have had to fill the void. They are all good players in their own right, but as it stands Chelsea do not have a strong midfield pairing with vast experience of either playing together, or even occupying that position.

Right across the team there has been a lot of change, and that is almost certain to create teething issues. Conceding twice from set pieces already and looking quite nervy from balls sent into the box, there is a sense that Alonso’s men have some work to do on their defensive game.
FACTS AND STATS
We are unbeaten in our last nine Premier League matches against Chelsea (W6 D3), our best unbeaten run against the Blues since a run of 19 between 1995 and 2005.
Chelsea have lost their last four away Premier League games against us by an aggregate score of 11-2. Their last win there was in August 2021, a 2-0 victory.

We have lost just one of their last 29 Premier League London derbies (W22 D6) and are unbeaten in their last 16 (W12 D4). The last side to have a longer unbeaten run was us between August 2022 and November 2023 (17 games).

Chelsea have started 2026-27 with three consecutive wins in all competitions (two in the Premier League, one in the League Cup). The Blues last won their opening four games to a season in 2016-17 (Antonio Conte’s first four) and their opening three Premier League games in 2018-19 (under Maurizio Sarri).
We have won our first two Premier League matches this season but only once in the last 21 seasons have we started our campaign with three wins, doing so in 2022/23.

Chelsea’s two Premier League matches this season have seen 12 goals (seven for, five against), the joint-third most in a side’s first two games of a campaign in the competition, behind only us in 2004/05 (13) and Leeds United in 2020/21 (14). They could become the first side to see their opening three games of a top-flight season all have 5+ goals since Arsenal in 1988-89.
Across the first two matchdays of 2026/27, we faced the fewest shots (11), the fewest shots on target (one) and allowed our opponents the lowest xG (0.54) of any Premier League side.
Since 2022/23, we have had 16 games where our opponents haven’t had a shot on target – twice as many as any other side (Liverpool, eight).

Bukayo Saka has scored in each of his last two Premier League appearances, last scoring more consecutively in January/February 2024 (five in a row). The last player to score in their first three games in a season was Alexandre Lacazette in 2020/21.
MATCH OFFICIALS

Chris Kavanagh is the man with the whistle for the London derby. He has taken charge of this fixture on two previous occasions, the most recent coming in March 2025, when Mikel Merino scored the winner in a 1-0 victory for us.
Kavanagh has refereed one game so far this season, a 1-1 draw between Bournemouth and Everton. The last time he officiated an Arsenal match was in May 2026, when we beat West Ham United 1-0.
Referee: Chris KavanaghAssistants: Dan Cook, Tim WoodFourth official: Tom BramallVAR: Darren EnglandAssistant VAR: Constantine Hatzidakis
CHELSEA RECORD
Since losing to Chelsea in August 2021, we've enjoyed an incredible 11-game unbeaten run against the Blues, spanning five years and nine different managers, interim or permanent, at the helm.
Those 11 unbeaten games have come across the Premier League and Carabao Cup, where we ousted the Blues 4-2 on aggregate in last season's semi-final.
Our last victory against Chelsea took place in March 2026, when William Saliba and Jurrien Timber headed us to victory at Emirates Stadium.
LIVE COVERAGE
A return to Emirates Stadium can only mean one thing, our preview show is back, Live from N5.

Packed with special guests, analysis and much more, head to Arsenal.com and The Arsenal app (download now on iOS/Android) for our preview show. Then, just before kick-off, tune in to Dan Roebuck and Adrian Clarke to take you through the on-field action against the Blues.
You can also find out which broadcasters are showing the action live, wherever you are in the world.

bodyEn: Control v chaos. On the one hand, the forces of order, regimented, playing in precise patterns and, on the other, something darker, more visceral, a method that acknowledges the imperfection of the human soul, the unknowability of football in all its randomness; better, that second way says, to attempt to ride the fury than to believe it might be harnessed.

When it began, a decade ago, that’s how the Pep Guardiola v Jürgen Klopp rivalry appeared. Apollo v Dionysius. Two fundamentally opposed ways of seeing the world. But in time, the two crept towards each other. Klopp moved away from the heavy metal of his Borussia Dortmund years to something more conservative. Guardiola experimented in multiple directions, slowly abandoning the possession-oriented idealism of his past to something less radical but also less predictable.

The temptation, after the first two weeks of the season, is to cast Mikel Arteta and Xabi Alonso in a similar light. Arsenal are yet to concede a goal. They dominated the Community Shield from the first minute, beat a shambolic Manchester City 3-0 and gave the sense that they could easily have won more comprehensively had they been minded to do so. They were no more troubled in beating Coventry by the same scoreline in their opening league game and, while they were rather less dominant, they were still extremely comfortable against Aston Villa on Monday and had been slowly increasing the pressure when Bukayo Saka gave them the lead just before the hour.

Arteta has become more controlling over his seven years at Arsenal, not just in his micromanagement but in his demands from his team. Tactical plans are sophisticated and negotiable only in the final details. In their third successive season of finishing second he spoke repeatedly of the need to reduce, to zero if possible, the xG of the opposition. If they have no chances, they cannot score, and if they do not score, they cannot win.

Last season it was a refrain heard less often; Arsenal did reduce their opponents’ opportunities, conceding seven goals fewer than they had the previous season. There were those who criticised them on aesthetic grounds, bemoaning their reliance on set plays and occasional bouts of excessive pragmatism, but it worked. They were the best team and they won the league, in the end, fairly comfortably. All else is taste, subjective.

Might, it will be asked, there be a more expansive approach this season? Might, with the burdens of yearning and doubt lifted, the insistence on control lessen? Might this be a breezier, a freer and easier, Arsenal? Might that even make them more effective in Europe, more capable of beating Paris Saint-Germain?

Probably not. Arsenal played as they did in the Champions League final out of necessity, not choice. They were exhausted. Only three PSG players had played more than 2,000 minutes in the league last season; nine Arsenal players had – and given the relative strengths of the Premier League and Ligue 1, theirs were harder minutes. In such circumstances an open game is impossible.

Accepting the role played by fatigue, in fact, has been one of Arsenal’s great strengths; last summer’s business was characterised by the accumulation of squad depth over acquisition of the very highest quality. This summer has been about upgrading where possible. They’ve seemingly done that well in midfield and at the back, although losing three players who can operate from the left wing while signing only Christos Tzolis seems a risk, even with Max Dowman likely to be more involved. It’s possible, likely even, that a more relaxed outlook will allow Arsenal to play with a greater freedom but it would be a surprise if the tactical emphasis were not still on control.

Chelsea’s case is more complex; the sense of chaos of Alonso’s opening two games has surely not been deliberate. He is no Kloppite; his heritage is of John Toshack and Rafa Benítez, Vicente Del Bosque and Guardiola. Like Arteta, four months his junior, he came through the youth ranks at Antiguoko in San Sebastián; they are not so different in their formation. When Alonso won the league at Bayer Leverkusen, they had 62% possession. Although they pressed hard, they were not part of the high-tempo, high-turnover Bundesliga trend. Yet in beating Fulham 3-2, Chelsea had 38% possession, and in beating Brighton 4-3 they had only 26%.

Game state is partly responsible. In both games, Chelsea had the lead early and could afford to allow their opponents the ball. The front three of João Pedro, Cole Palmer and Morgan Rogers have excelled playing on the break. There have been glimmers of the sort of interactions Leverkusen produced, the modifications that prevent Alonso’s 3-4-2-1 from experiencing the blockishness that means the formation is more often a tool for counterattacking sides, most notably when Maxence Lacroix advanced from central defence to set up Rogers’ goal against Fulham. But they take time to develop; perhaps the idea for now, as patterns are assimilated, is to lean into the basic simplicity of shape, the security the two screening midfielders in front of the back three should offer.

The problem is, it hasn’t yet worked – although that may in part be down to personnel. Having sold Enzo Fernández without signing another central midfielder, though, Chelsea look short in midfield (in as much their bloated squad can look short of anything). If Roméo Lavia can remain fit, and if Reece James’s minutes can continue to be rationed, the issue should not be insoluble, but Moisés Caicedo’s knee problem complicates things, especially with Alonso seemingly unwilling yet to trust the 22-year-old Argentinian Valentín Barco from the start. Without Caicedo, that is not a midfield that is going to create much, and may struggle even with ball retention.

It’s possible that on Sunday, in a game Chelsea are not expected to win, it is easier to maintain shape and discipline, that a destructive pairing works more naturally. Only by making the game a midfield slog to be decided by which team’s forward line can best exploit breakdowns can Chelsea feel they have an edge. That may end up looking like control against chaos, like possession against turnovers. It may even be so. But for Alonso that is a matter less of ideology than of expediency.

items.titleEn: Smith hails "hungry" young Gunners
items.summaryEn: Our under-18s coach reflects on our first win of the season against Southampton
bodyEn: Under-18s coach Josh Smith was pleased with his side’s spirited performance against Southampton, securing their first three points of the season.
Maalik Hashi scored the only goal of the game inside 15 minutes with a neat finish off the post and our young Gunners held on despite late Saints pressure.

"I thought it was a very positive start to the game. We've been speaking to the boys about how they start and today we had seven corners in the first 10 minutes, so in terms of how we started the game, it was very pleasing.

"In the first half, the build-up, finding the free player, using the third man and the entries into the final third were probably the best that we've seen. We're trying to encourage Mal [Maalik Hashi] to shoot from distance and have our midfielders arrive late into the box to score, so really pleased for Mal today.

"Second half, I thought it was a game where, if we take our chances, it could be two, three or four. I think the decision-making in the second half, sort of in and around the box, not taking those chances, gave Southampton a little bit of hope. But in terms of how the lads reacted and how we had to defend, we're pleased."
Our strong start was enough to earn our first U18 Premier League South win of the campaign, with our work in front of goal proving decisive.
Josh was pleased with the way we controlled the opening half, while admitting there was room for greater consistency after the interval.

"I thought there was a clear style in terms of how we built up and how we entered the final third, especially in the first half. Some of our decision-making, whether to play through or round over, and the technical execution of the players, was clean today.

“However, in the second half, I was a little bit disappointed because when we did win the ball back, we needed to judge whether it was a fast moment to go or whether we needed to slow it down. It was a contrast between the two halves, but for us as staff, we need to demand more consistency across both halves.”
Despite a tricky start to the season, Josh has also been encouraged by the group's progress during the opening weeks, with performances suggesting results would come.

The academy coach was delighted to see their efforts beat a Southampton side that entered the game with three wins from three. "I see a hungry group of players," he said. "Every single day they come into training and bring a mindset that they want to get better. That's all we can ask for from these young scholars.

"I see a real kind of perseverance in sticking to what we're doing. Recently, players and staff have been feeling a little down with the results, but we believe we can continue what we're doing and turn those performances into good results. I'm really, really pleased for the boys today."

bodyEn: For many people connected to Arsenal, it has been a time to remember the old line from Arsène Wenger. “We live in a society of ‘news’,” the club’s former manager once said, and by that he meant new things – the shinier the better.

Nowhere is the obsession more obvious than in the transfer market, when a club simply has to add new faces. These days, it feels as though some fans prefer them to be signed as late as possible in the summer window to ensure a positive narrative after the deadline; to maximise the potential to generate momentum. Recency bias is powerful.

Wenger’s tone was disapproving. The next big thing is not always thus. What you already have should not be undervalued or taken for granted. It struck a chord with Mikel Arteta, which everybody in the room for his press conference to preview Sunday’s home game against Chelsea could feel because it moved him out of succinct answer territory.

The Arsenal manager enters the match having won three out of three this season – including the Community Shield victory over Manchester City – without conceding a goal. His club, of course, ended their long wait for the Premier League title last May when they chased away all manner of demons. They are hot favourites to win it again.

At Aston Villa on Monday night, Arteta introduced two of Spain’s World Cup winning squad – Mikel Merino and Martín Zubimendi – from the bench. Plus the marquee summer signing, Bruno Guimarães. Plus Eberechi Eze. Plus another high-profile new boy, Ezri Konsa. Arsenal’s strength in depth is really something.

Their squad is surely stronger now than it was at the end of last season. Does Arteta feel that? “Yes I do,” he said. “We are better equipped. We have more players available. We have increased the quality and we have increased the leadership in the team as well, which is very important.”

So, why the angst among supporters after the transfer window closed, which was probably nearer to hysteria in some cases? “It’s human nature,” Arteta said. “When you talk to people and you ask them … normally, it’s: ‘OK, what is on your bucket list?’ People write a lot about the bucket list. And sometimes we forget the reverse bucket list, which is the things that you already have in your life that are incredible. But you put so much emphasis on them [the bucket list items] that nothing seems to be enough.

“It’s very important to value what we have, what we have created together. To have ambition is great, especially to evolve the things we already have within the club. But listen – don’t lose perspective to what we already have, which is amazing.”

Arsenal are indisputably better in defence with Konsa and in midfield with Guimarães. The worry is the front line where it has been one in (Christos Tzolis) and four out (Leandro Trossard, Gabriel Martinelli, Gabriel Jesus and Ethan Nwaneri).

The reasoning for each departure was difficult to fault. Trossard is 31, he had one year on his contract and Besiktas offered £15.3m. Tzolis felt like a fine replacement for him. Martinelli scored once in the league last season, although he contributed four in the FA Cup and six in the Champions League. Arsenal got £60m from Al-Hilal for him; a club record sale.

As an aside, Arteta mentioned how Arsenal had “made a move last summer” – a reference to their lavish spending – and there has been an acknowledgement within the club that there had to be a balancing this time.

Jesus started nine games in all competitions last season, scoring six goals. He, too, was into the final year of his deal, and he was one of the club’s highest earners. At one stage, it looked as though he might look to see out his contract and in the end, a £8.6m deal with Barcelona rising to £12.9m suited all parties. Nwaneri barely played for Arsenal last season, going to Marseille on loan in January. Another loan, this time to Borussia Dortmund, made sense, particularly as there is a January recall clause.

Yet the weight of the outgoing numbers makes it hard to say Arsenal are stronger in this department and Arteta was in no mood to over-promise here. “It’s another question and we have to prove in that particular position whether we are better or not,” he said. “Let’s see. I understand the point of view [about the number of departures] but we have to understand as well the amount of minutes that those players played. And the ones that were injured last season, especially in the first six months. It is what it is.”

There is the belief at Arsenal that Eze can in essence replace Martinelli on the left, albeit he is a different kind of player. Arsenal can perhaps play in a different way, with Riccardo Calafiori stepping up more from left-back. There is the hope that with a reshaped medical staff, the team can have a better run on the injury front – specifically with Bukayo Saka, Martin Ødegaard and Kai Havertz having uninterrupted seasons. The fear is that more problems will undermine them.

What has coloured the post-transfer window vibe is the failure to add a big-name attacker, to make a real statement signing. If Arteta did have a bucket list, then a game-changer for the front line would have been on it. Arsenal did try; they reached for stars such as Vinícius Júnior, Julián Alvarez and Morgan Rogers. Arteta even suggested that this kind of intent was progress. It is a tough sell when the glamour targets remain elusive.

There was a point in July when Arsenal thought there was more of a chance they would get Vinícius than not. Then Real Madrid made him a new contract offer and he signed it. Alvarez just did not want to come, and the case of Rogers boiled down to the numbers. Arsenal offered £80m to Aston Villa for him and no more. Chelsea ended up going to £117m. They overpaid. But then they announced a deal with Villa two days later to loan Alejandro Garnacho there with a conditional purchase obligation, valuing the winger at £40m. Chelsea found a way to get Rogers. Arsenal did not. He will be a major subplot on Sunday .

There were moments when Arteta dropped his usual ultra-positive outlook and offered little peeks behind the curtain, including when he suggested that reporters speak to the sporting director, Andrea Berta, or the co-chair Josh Kroenke about why it was so difficult to close deals for the very elite.

“To get these deals done in this market is complicated,” he said. “I don’t know how it looks from the outside but we have put in everything that we possibly could to make those deals happen and we made most of them happen. We have been very efficient with what Andrea has done in the market again. It has been incredible, the support of all the club and that’s it. It’s not perfect but it doesn’t need to be perfect.”
Arteta believes that Arsenal have enough.

bodyEn: Chelsea thought they had little chance of signing Morgan Rogers at the start of the summer. Xabi Alonso and the club’s recruitment team had the England international as a priority target but a deal seemed unlikely. Chelsea had endured a disappointing season, missing out on European football after finishing 10th, and their expectation was that Rogers would leave Aston Villa for Arsenal.

It was towards the end of the World Cup that Chelsea were made aware of a window of opportunity. Although Arsenal could claim to be London’s top dogs after winning the Premier League they dithered in talks with Villa, raising the prospect of another club stepping in.

Mikel Arteta talked about being bold in the market after Arsenal’s defeat by Paris Saint-Germain in the Champions League final. Arteta wanted more in attack. A new option on the left was a priority; Leandro Trossard and Gabriel Martinelli were up for sale and everything pointed towards Arsenal making their move for Rogers at the end of June.

Yet the lines became blurred. Arsenal had a fee of £80m in mind, while Villa wanted more, particularly after Nottingham Forest sold Elliot Anderson to Manchester City for £116m. Time dragged on. How serious were Arsenal? There was also interest in Julián Alvarez, Vinícius Júnior and Bradley Barcola. Villa waited and the price for Rogers went up. Arsenal, beaten to the punch in the end, will have a look at what they could have won when Chelsea and Rogers visit the Emirates Stadium on Sunday.

Chelsea were decisive. They were tracking Rogers before he left Middlesbrough for Villa in February 2024. Joe Shields, one of Chelsea’s five sporting directors, worked with Rogers at Manchester City’s academy. The signing was not done on a whim. Chelsea have a good relationship with Villa’s owners and moved quickly after opening club-to-club talks a day after Rogers played in England’s World Cup semi-final defeat by Argentina. The fee was £117m and Chelsea did not struggle to convince Rogers. Alonso wooed him and the deal was confirmed five days after negotiations began.

There was no last-ditch move from Arsenal. They signed Christos Tzolis from Club Brugge for £34m two days later and focused on other targets. When the window closed, though, Arteta’s options on the left looked a little light. Martinelli and Trossard left but only Tzolis arrived. Eberechi Eze and Noni Madueke are alternatives. It is hard not to feel that Arsenal could have done with Rogers, even though Chelsea have paid a high price for him.

It remains to be seen whether the 24-year-old can prove he merits becoming the third-most expensive player in English football history. For context, the fee is the consequence of the market threatening to rise out of control and the money spent on many players starting to feel meaningless. It is worth pointing out, too, that money flowed back and forth between Chelsea and Villa all summer. Even so the price will follow Rogers around, so it is just as well he has made an excellent start.

Rogers has been involved in four of Chelsea’s seven goals in their first two league games. He scored in the 3-2 win at Fulham and later combined with João Pedro to set up Cole Palmer’s goal. He created Pedro Neto’s goal in last weekend’s 4-3 win over Brighton and played a key role when Jorrel Hato played in João Pedro to score.

Chelsea have thrilled in attack so far, João Pedro, Rogers and Palmer combining to devastating effect. Alonso, an adaptable manager, wants more control but his transitional football has been a delight. Chelsea were mannered and controlled during Enzo Maresca’s time in charge. It is felt that Alonso has recognised the Premier League’s shift towards power and athleticism. Rogers fits into the Spaniard’s system. Thomas Tuchel loves Rogers for his connectivity and pressing. It is significant that England’s energy levels rose in their quarter-final against Norway after the introduction of Rogers and Djed Spence late in the second half.

Chelsea needed more strength, more speed. Rogers, able to play anywhere in attacking midfield or as a No 8, looks a better fit in Alonso’s 3-4-2-1 than Enzo Fernández, sold this week to Manchester City for £125m. He has played with Palmer as one of the No 10s but has a responsibility to drift left, a role that is unlikely to have suited Fernández. Arsenal’s impeccable defence will be tested by Chelsea’s front three.

The Rogers-Palmer partnership has clicked. They are old friends and banter over the “ice cold” celebration. Rogers is a bubbly character and can get on with anyone. Chelsea are keen to improve the culture in the dressing room. It is felt that Alonso has shifted the mood after last year’s rebellions. The squad are united. It is one of the reasons why Chelsea decided to sell Fernández on deadline day. They did not need the headache of reintegrating the Argentinian.

This is a fresh start. The signing of Rogers, who was the Professional Footballers’ Association’s young player of the year in 2025, was a sign of Chelsea’s intent. Rogers was one of the best players in the Premier League last season. He grew under Unai Emery and scored when Villa beat Freiburg in the Europa League final in May.

It was one of Rogers’ less eye-catching goals: a clever jab at the near post from a low cross. There was a period last season when he could not stop scoring from long range but Rogers has spoken about wanting scruffier goals and he arrived at the far post to open his Chelsea account against Fulham.

Rogers is embracing the challenge. At Arsenal he would have been slotting into the finished article. Arsenal have reached the summit. Chelsea are beginning their climb under Alonso. Rogers, who has played in the Championship and had a loan in League One, rather liked the idea of starting lower down.

items.titleEn: Premier League: 10 things to look out for this weekend
